title: Ὁ ἱστὸς καὶ ἡ Κρήτη
titleEn: Penelope’s Web and the Tale of Crete — Odyssey 19.104–202
part: Penelope’s Web and the Tale of Crete (19.104–202)
about: Penelope asks the stranger who he is and where he is from. Odysseus answers that her fame is like that of a just king, and begs her not to question his birth, since it will only renew his grief. She replies with her own sorrow: the gods ruined her beauty when Odysseus sailed, the lords of all the islands are wooing her against her will, and she tells how she put them off for three years with a robe woven by day and unwoven by night, until the maids gave her away. Now she cannot escape marriage, her parents urge it, and her son is angry at the loss of his property, so she asks again for his family. Odysseus warns her that the telling will hurt, and begins a tale of Crete: he is Aethon, younger brother of Idomeneus, and he once entertained Odysseus, whom the North Wind kept in Crete for twelve days. The tale runs on into the next part.

sentences.t: ξεῖνε, τὸ μέν σε πρῶτον ἐγὼν εἰρήσομαι αὐτή·
sentences.l: “Stranger, this first I will ask you, I myself:
sentences.i: “Stranger, this is what I myself shall ask you first:
sentences.n: Penelope puts her question to the stranger herself. τὸ … πρῶτον is ‘this first’ (τό is the article used as a pronoun), ἐγών is the Epic form of ἐγώ ‘I’, and αὐτή ‘myself’ stresses that she asks in person. εἰρήσομαι is the future of εἴρομαι ‘ask’, with σε ‘you’ and τό as its two objects.

sentences.t: τίς πόθεν εἶς ἀνδρῶν; πόθι τοι πόλις ἠδὲ τοκῆες;
sentences.l: Who among men are you, and from where? Where is your city and your parents?”
sentences.i: Who among men are you, and where from? Where is your city, and where are your parents?”
sentences.n: Two questions in one line. τίς … πόθεν is ‘who … from where’; εἶς is the Epic form of εἶ ‘you are’; ἀνδρῶν is partitive, ‘among men’. The second question uses πόθι ‘where’ (a place, not ‘from where’), τοι for σοι ‘your’, and τοκῆες ‘parents’; this second question has no verb (‘is’ is understood). Her speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: The formula for an answer, spoken now by Odysseus, who is still unrecognised: τὴν … ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering her’ (ἀπαμείβομαι ‘answer’), with προσέφη ‘addressed’, and τήν is the article used as a pronoun, ‘her’. The stock epithet πολύμητις, ‘of many wiles’ (μῆτις is craft, cunning), is translated every time.

sentences.t:
ὦ γύναι, οὐκ ἄν τίς σε βροτῶν ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν
νεικέοι·
sentences.l:
“O woman, no one of mortals, over the boundless earth,
could find fault with you;
sentences.i: “O woman, no mortal anywhere on the boundless earth could find fault with you;
sentences.n: Odysseus begins with a compliment. γύναι is the plain ‘woman’, a courteous way for a stranger to address a lady, and ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν is ‘over the boundless earth’. οὐκ ἄν τίς σε … νεικέοι is a potential optative, ‘no one could find fault with you’ (νεικέοι is the 3 sg. optative of νεικέω ‘quarrel with, blame’), with βροτῶν partitive, ‘of mortals’. The reason follows, introduced by ἦ γάρ.

sentences.t:
ἦ γάρ σευ κλέος οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἱκάνει,
ὥς τέ τευ ἢ βασιλῆος ἀμύμονος, ὅς τε θεουδὴς
ἀνδράσιν ἐν πολλοῖσι καὶ ἰφθίμοισιν ἀνάσσων
εὐδικίας ἀνέχῃσι,
sentences.l:
for truly your fame reaches the wide heaven,
as of some one, or of a blameless king, who, god-fearing,
among men many and mighty ruling,
upholds just judgements,
sentences.i: for your fame, truly, reaches the wide sky, like the fame of some blameless king who, god-fearing and ruling over many mighty men, upholds just judgements,
sentences.n: The reason for the praise, as a simile. σευ is the Epic σοῦ, so σευ κλέος is ‘your fame’, and οὐρανὸν εὐρύν is ‘the wide heaven’ (‘sky’ in the easy English). ὥς τέ τευ ἢ βασιλῆος is ‘like that of some one, or of a king’ (τευ is Epic τινός; the exact force of ἤ is not certain, but the sense is ‘like a king’s’). ἀμύμων ‘blameless’ is a stock epithet whose meaning is not known; θεουδής is ‘god-fearing’, ἰφθίμοισιν ‘mighty’. ὅς τε … ἀνέχῃσι is a general relative clause (subjunctive, ‘who upholds’), and εὐδικίας, accusative plural, is its object.

sentences.t:
φέρῃσι δὲ γαῖα μέλαινα
πυροὺς καὶ κριθάς, βρίθῃσι δὲ δένδρεα καρπῷ,
τίκτῃ δ’ ἔμπεδα μῆλα, θάλασσα δὲ παρέχῃ ἰχθῦς
ἐξ εὐηγεσίης, ἀρετῶσι δὲ λαοὶ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ.
sentences.l:
and bears the dark earth
wheat and barley, and the trees are heavy with fruit,
and the flocks bear steadily, and the sea provides fish,
from good leading, and the peoples prosper under him.
sentences.i: and the dark earth bears wheat and barley, the trees are heavy with fruit, the flocks bear without fail, and the sea provides fish, from good leadership, and the peoples prosper under him.
sentences.n: The picture of the just king’s land. The subjunctives φέρῃσι, βρίθῃσι, τίκτῃ, παρέχῃ carry on the general relative clause of the last unit, ‘under whom …’. γαῖα μέλαινα is ‘the dark earth’, πυροί ‘wheat’, κριθαί ‘barley’; βρίθω is ‘be heavy’, with καρπῷ ‘with fruit’; μῆλα (neuter plural) is the subject of the singular τίκτῃ, ‘bear young’, and ἔμπεδα ‘steadily’. εὐηγεσίη, ‘good leading’, is a rare word built from εὖ and ἡγέομαι; ἀρετῶσι ‘they thrive’ is from ἀρετάω, a rare verb whose sense comes from the context.

sentences.t:
τῷ ἐμὲ νῦν τὰ μὲν ἄλλα μετάλλα σῷ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ,
μηδ’ ἐμὸν ἐξερέεινε γένος καὶ πατρίδα γαῖαν,
μή μοι μᾶλλον θυμὸν ἐνιπλήσῃς ὀδυνάων
μνησαμένῳ μάλα δ’ εἰμὶ πολύστονος·
sentences.l:
Therefore me now, as to other matters, ask in your own house,
and do not inquire into my birth and fatherland,
lest you fill my heart the more with pains
as I remember; for very much-groaning am I;
sentences.i: So ask me now about other things in your own house, and do not question me about my birth and my fatherland, lest you fill my heart with still more pain as I remember; for I am a man of many groans;
sentences.n: Odysseus declines to tell his birth. τῷ is ‘therefore’; μετάλλα and ἐξερέεινε are imperatives (‘ask’, ‘inquire into’), the second negated by μηδ’. μή μοι … ἐνιπλήσῃς is ‘lest you fill’ (aorist subjunctive of ἐμπίμπλημι, with the genitive ὀδυνάων ‘with pains’); μνησαμένῳ, dative agreeing with μοι, is ‘as I remember’. πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘fatherland’, and πολύστονος ‘full of groans’ (στόνος ‘groan’).

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί με χρὴ
οἴκῳ ἐν ἀλλοτρίῳ γοόωντά τε μυρόμενόν τε
ἧσθαι, ἐπεὶ κάκιον πενθήμεναι ἄκριτον αἰεί·
sentences.i: and I ought not to sit in another’s house wailing and lamenting, since it is worse to grieve endlessly, always;
sentences.n: οὐδέ τί με χρή is ‘nor ought I at all’: χρή takes the accusative με and the infinitive ἧσθαι ‘to sit’. γοόωντα, from γοάω, and μυρόμενον, from μύρομαι, are ‘wailing’ and ‘lamenting’, both agreeing with με. ἀλλοτρίῳ is ‘another’s’, not his own. πενθήμεναι is the Epic infinitive of πενθέω ‘mourn’, κάκιον the comparative ‘worse’, and ἄκριτον, here an adverb, ‘without end’.

sentences.t:
μή τίς μοι δμῳῶν νεμεσήσεται, ἠὲ σύ γ’ αὐτή,
φῇ δὲ δακρυπλώειν βεβαρηότα με φρένας οἴνῳ.
sentences.l:
lest some one of the maids feel indignation at me, or you yourself,
and say that I swim in tears, weighed down in my wits with wine.”
sentences.i: lest one of the maids feel indignation at me — or you yourself — and say that I am swimming in tears, my wits weighed down with wine.”
sentences.n: μή … νεμεσήσεται (future in form, though it may be read as a short-vowel subjunctive) is ‘lest … feel indignation at me’ (νεμεσάω; the verb recurs in line 146); φῇ, subjunctive of φημί, continues it, ‘and say’. The subjects are τίς δμῳῶν ‘one of the maids’ and, after ἠέ, σύ γ’ αὐτή ‘you yourself’. δακρυπλώειν is ‘to swim in tears’ (δάκρυ ‘tear’ and πλώω ‘float, swim’); βεβαρηότα, perfect participle of βαρέω, is ‘weighed down’, with φρένας ‘in my wits’ and οἴνῳ ‘with wine’. Odysseus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.l: Him then answered circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope answered him:
sentences.n: Penelope answers him. τόν is the article used as a pronoun, ‘him’; ἠμείβετο is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, with ἔπειτα ‘then’. The epithet περίφρων, ‘circumspect’, is Penelope’s stock epithet and is translated every time.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, ἦ τοι μὲν ἐμὴν ἀρετὴν εἶδός τε δέμας τε
ὤλεσαν ἀθάνατοι, ὅτε Ἴλιον εἰσανέβαινον
Ἀργεῖοι, μετὰ τοῖσι δ’ ἐμὸς πόσις ᾖεν Ὀδυσσεύς
εἰ κεῖνός γ’ ἐλθὼν τὸν ἐμὸν βίον ἀμφιπολεύοι,
μεῖζον κε κλέος εἴη ἐμὸν καὶ κάλλιον οὕτως.
sentences.i: “Stranger, the immortals destroyed my excellence, my form and my body, when the Argives went up to Ilium, and among them went my husband Odysseus; if he came back and watched over my life, my fame would be greater and finer in that way.
sentences.n: Penelope answers with her own grief. ἦ τοι μέν is ‘truly indeed’; ἀρετήν, εἶδος and δέμας (‘excellence’, ‘form’, ‘body’) are all objects of ὤλεσαν ‘destroyed’, whose subject ἀθάνατοι ‘the immortals’ follows it, as Ἀργεῖοι ‘the Argives’ follows εἰσανέβαινον ‘were going up (into Ilium)’. ᾖεν is the imperfect of εἶμι, ‘went’. εἰ … ἀμφιπολεύοι with κε … εἴη is a condition, ‘if he were to tend my life, my fame would be greater’. The edition prints no stop after Ὀδυσσεύς at the end of line 126; the semicolon is ours.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἄχομαι· τόσα γάρ μοι ἐπέσσευεν κακὰ δαίμων.
sentences.l: But now I grieve; for so many against me drove evils some power.
sentences.i: But now I grieve, for some power has driven so many evils upon me.
sentences.n: Why she grieves. ἄχομαι is ‘I am distressed, I grieve’. τόσα … κακά, ‘so many evils’, is the object of ἐπέσσευεν, the Epic form (doubled σ) of ἐπέσευεν, ‘drove upon’, with μοι ‘upon me’. δαίμων is ‘some power’, an unnamed divine force.

sentences.t:
ὅσσοι γὰρ νήσοισιν ἐπικρατέουσιν ἄριστοι,
Δουλιχίῳ τε Σάμῃ τε καὶ ὑλήεντι Ζακύνθῳ,
οἵ τ’ αὐτὴν Ἰθάκην εὐδείελον ἀμφινέμονται,
οἵ μ’ ἀεκαζομένην μνῶνται, τρύχουσι δὲ οἶκον.
sentences.l:
For as many as hold power over the islands, the best men,
over Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus,
and who dwell around Ithaca itself, clear-seen,
they woo me, much against my will, and wear out the house.
sentences.i: For all the chief men who hold power in the islands, in Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus, and those who live round about clear-seen Ithaca itself — they are wooing me, much against my will, and wearing out the house.
sentences.n: Penelope names the suitors’ homelands. ὅσσοι … ἄριστοι is ‘as many as are best’, the subject, with ἐπικρατέουσιν ‘hold power over’ and the datives νήσοισιν, Δουλιχίῳ, Σάμῃ, Ζακύνθῳ naming the places. οἵ τ’ … ἀμφινέμονται is a second relative clause, ‘and who dwell round about’, with αὐτήν ‘Ithaca itself’ and εὐδείελον ‘clear-seen’; the old derivations conflict (from δείελος ‘evening’ or δῆλος ‘visible’), so the literal word is kept. The next οἵ picks them all up again, ‘they’; ἀεκαζομένην agrees with μ’ (‘me’), ‘against my will’.

sentences.t:
τῷ οὔτε ξείνων ἐμπάζομαι οὔθ’ ἱκετάων
οὔτε τι κηρύκων, οἳ δημιοεργοὶ ἔασιν·
sentences.l:
Therefore neither for strangers do I care, nor for suppliants,
nor at all for heralds, who are craftsmen for the people;
sentences.i: That is why I pay no heed to strangers or suppliants, or to heralds, who are craftsmen for the people;
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘therefore’: the suitors’ doings leave her no heart for these duties. ἐμπάζομαι takes the genitive, ‘I pay heed to’; ξείνων ‘strangers’, ἱκετάων (Epic genitive plural of ἱκέτης, ‘suppliants’) and κηρύκων ‘heralds’ are what she does not heed, with οὔτε … οὔθ’ … οὔτε τι ‘neither … nor … nor at all’. δημιοεργοί are those who work for the community (δῆμος ‘people, land’, ἔργον ‘work’); the house rendering ‘craftsmen for the people’ is kept even of heralds. ἔασιν is the Epic form of εἰσίν.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ Ὀδυσῆ ποθέουσα φίλον κατατήκομαι ἦτορ.
sentences.l: but for Odysseus longing, I melt away in my dear heart.
sentences.i: but longing for Odysseus, I waste away at heart.
sentences.n: ἀλλά ‘but’ sets her longing against her indifference to the guests. ποθέουσα, from ποθέω ‘long for’, takes the accusative Ὀδυσῆ(α), elided here; κατατήκομαι is ‘I melt away, waste away’; φίλον ἦτορ is an accusative of respect, ‘in my dear heart’ (the ‘dear’ is dropped in the easy English).

sentences.t: οἱ δὲ γάμον σπεύδουσιν· ἐγὼ δὲ δόλους τολυπεύω.
sentences.l: They hasten the marriage; but I wind up tricks.
sentences.i: They press on with the marriage, while I work out my tricks.
sentences.n: οἱ δέ … ἐγὼ δέ sets ‘they’ against ‘I’ (οἵ is the article used as a pronoun). σπεύδω with the accusative γάμον is ‘press on with, hasten’ the marriage. τολυπεύω is the wool-worker’s ‘wind into a ball’, here ‘work up, carry through’; δόλους is ‘tricks’. The tricks are the web she goes on to describe.

sentences.t:
φᾶρος μέν μοι πρῶτον ἐνέπνευσε φρεσὶ δαίμων,
στησαμένῃ μέγαν ἱστόν, ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ὑφαίνειν,
λεπτὸν καὶ περίμετρον·
sentences.i: First, some power put it into my mind to set up a great loom in the halls and weave a robe, fine and very large;
sentences.n: The first trick: the robe. φᾶρος … ὑφαίνειν is ‘to weave a robe’, the object set first for emphasis; ἐνέπνευσε φρεσί is ‘breathed into my wits’, that is, put the idea into her mind. μοι and the participle στησαμένῃ (‘having set up’, dative feminine) go together, ‘for me, who had set up’. λεπτόν is ‘fine’ and περίμετρον ‘very large’ (περί- ‘very’, μέτρον ‘measure’), a rare word. δαίμων is ‘some power’.

sentences.t: ἄφαρ δ’ αὐτοῖς μετέειπον·
sentences.l: and straightway among them I spoke:
sentences.i: And at once I spoke among them:
sentences.n: A first-person speech-introduction: μετέειπον is ‘I spoke among’, with the dative αὐτοῖς ‘to them’, the suitors; ἄφαρ is ‘straightway’. What she then said to them is quoted in the next units, in single marks, a speech inside her speech.

sentences.t: κοῦροι, ἐμοὶ μνηστῆρες, ἐπεὶ θάνε δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
sentences.l: ‘Young men, my suitors, since heavenly Odysseus has died,
sentences.i: ‘Young men, my suitors, since heavenly Odysseus is dead,
sentences.n: The words Penelope says she spoke to the suitors begin here and run to line 147. κοῦροι, ἐμοὶ μνηστῆρες is ‘young men, my suitors’ (ἐμοί, ‘to me’, does the work of ‘my’). θάνε is the unaugmented aorist ‘died’ of θνῄσκω, and δῖος is the stock ‘heavenly’ of Odysseus, translated every time.

sentences.t:
μίμνετ’ ἐπειγόμενοι τὸν ἐμὸν γάμον, εἰς ὅ κε φᾶρος
ἐκτελέσω—μή μοι μεταμώνια νήματ’ ὄληται—
Λαέρτῃ ἥρωϊ ταφήϊον, εἰς ὅτε κέν μιν
μοῖρ’ ὀλοὴ καθέλῃσι τανηλεγέος θανάτοιο·
sentences.l:
wait, eager though you are for my marriage, until this robe
I finish — lest my threads should perish, gone to waste —
for the hero Laertes a burial-cloth, against the time when him
the deadly fate takes down of death that lays-at-length;
sentences.i: wait, eager though you are for my marriage, until I have finished this robe — so that my spinning may not be wasted and lost — as a shroud for the hero Laertes, against the day when the deadly fate of death that lays men at length shall take him down;
sentences.n: The pretext: a burial-cloth. μίμνετε is the imperative ‘wait’, ἐπειγόμενοι ‘pressing’ for τὸν ἐμὸν γάμον; εἰς ὅ κε φᾶρος ἐκτελέσω is ‘until I finish the robe’ (κε with the subjunctive), and μή μοι … ὄληται, set between dashes, ‘lest my threads perish’. ταφήϊον ‘burial-cloth’ stands in apposition to φᾶρος, and εἰς ὅτε κέν μιν … καθέλῃσι is ‘against the time when … shall take him down’. τανηλεγής, said of death, has no known meaning: ‘that lays at length’ is the usual guess, ‘bringing long sorrow’ the other.

sentences.t:
μή τίς μοι κατὰ δῆμον Ἀχαιϊάδων νεμεσήσῃ,
αἴ κεν ἄτερ σπείρου κεῖται πολλὰ κτεατίσσας.
sentences.l:
lest anyone in the land of the Achaean women feel indignation at me,
if without a winding-sheet he should lie, having won much.’
sentences.i: so that none of the Achaean women in the land may feel indignation at me, if he should lie without a winding-sheet, a man who had won great possessions.’
sentences.n: The reason for the pretext. μή τίς μοι … νεμεσήσῃ is ‘lest anyone feel indignation at me’; Ἀχαιϊάδων, genitive plural of Ἀχαιϊάς ‘Achaean woman’, goes with τίς, and κατὰ δῆμον is ‘throughout the land’. αἴ κεν (αἴ = εἰ) … κεῖται is ‘if he should lie’; ἄτερ σπείρου ‘without a winding-sheet’; κτεατίσσας, aorist participle of κτεατίζω, ‘having acquired’. The quoted speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, τοῖσιν δ’ ἐπεπείθετο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ.
sentences.l: So I spoke, and in them their manly spirit was persuaded.
sentences.i: So I spoke, and their proud spirits were won over.
sentences.n: Penelope returns to her own account after the quotation. ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘so I spoke’ (ἐφάμην, imperfect of φημί). θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ, a stock phrase, is ‘manly spirit’ (‘proud’ in the easy English) and the subject of ἐπεπείθετο ‘was persuaded’; τοῖσιν δ’ is ‘in them’, the suitors.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα καὶ ἠματίη μὲν ὑφαίνεσκον μέγαν ἱστόν,
νύκτας δ’ ἀλλύεσκον, ἐπεὶ δαΐδας παραθείμην.
sentences.l:
There by day I would weave the great web,
but by nights I would unravel it, when I had set torches beside me.
sentences.i: There by day I would weave my great web, and by night unravel it again, once I had placed torches beside me.
sentences.n: The routine. ὑφαίνεσκον and ἀλλύεσκον have the Epic iterative ending -σκ-, ‘would weave’, ‘would unravel’; ἠματίη is ‘by day’ and νύκτας ‘by night’ (accusative of time), ἱστός here the ‘web’ on the loom. ἐπεὶ … παραθείμην is the optative of repeated action, ‘whenever I had set (παρατίθημι) torches beside me’; δαΐδας is ‘torches’.

sentences.t: ὣς τρίετες μὲν ἔληθον ἐγὼ καὶ ἔπειθον Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.l: So for three years I kept escaping notice, I, and kept persuading the Achaeans;
sentences.i: So for three years I went unnoticed and kept persuading the Achaeans;
sentences.n: τρίετες is ‘for three years’. ἔληθον and ἔπειθον are imperfects, ‘I kept escaping notice’ (Epic λήθω, for λανθάνω) and ‘I kept persuading’, with ἐγώ ‘I’ stressed; ‘the Achaeans’ here are the suitors. μέν is balanced by the ἀλλά that opens the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε τέτρατον ἦλθεν ἔτος καὶ ἐπήλυθον ὧραι,
μηνῶν φθινόντων, περὶ δ’ ἤματα πόλλ’ ἐτελέσθη,
καὶ τότε δή με διὰ δμῳάς, κύνας οὐκ ἀλεγούσας,
εἷλον ἐπελθόντες καὶ ὁμόκλησαν ἐπέεσσιν.
sentences.l:
But when the fourth year came, and the seasons passed by,
as the months were waning, and many days were brought round to their end,
then indeed, through the maids, dogs that took no heed,
they caught me, coming upon me, and rebuked me with words.
sentences.i: But when the fourth year came round and the seasons had passed, as the months waned and many days had run their course, then, through the maids — dogs that took no heed — they caught me, coming upon me, and rebuked me with their words.
sentences.n: The trick is found out. μηνῶν φθινόντων is a genitive absolute, ‘the months waning’; περὶ … ἐτελέσθη is tmesis (the preverb set apart), ‘were completed (all round)’, said of the days coming to their count. διὰ δμῳάς is ‘through the maids’, κύνας οὐκ ἀλεγούσας ‘dogs, not heeding’ (ἀλέγω ‘heed, care for’). The subject of εἷλον ‘caught’ and ὁμόκλησαν ‘rebuked’ is not named: the suitors.

sentences.t: ὣς τὸ μὲν ἐξετέλεσσα, καὶ οὐκ ἐθέλουσ’, ὑπ’ ἀνάγκης·
sentences.l: So I finished it, even unwilling, under compulsion;
sentences.i: So I finished it, against my will, under compulsion;
sentences.n: τό is ‘it’, the robe. ἐξετέλεσσα is the Epic aorist (doubled σ) of ἐκτελέω ‘finish’; καὶ οὐκ ἐθέλουσ’ is ‘even though not willing’, the participle agreeing with the speaker, and ὑπ’ ἀνάγκης ‘under compulsion’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ οὔτ’ ἐκφυγέειν δύναμαι γάμον οὔτε τιν’ ἄλλην
μῆτιν ἔθ’ εὑρίσκω·
sentences.l:
But now neither to escape the marriage am I able, nor any other
plan do I still find;
sentences.i: But now I cannot escape the marriage, and I find no other plan any longer;
sentences.n: ἐκφυγέειν is the Epic infinitive of ἐκφεύγω ‘escape’ (Attic ἐκφυγεῖν), depending on δύναμαι ‘I am able’. οὔτε … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor’, and the negative carries over to εὑρίσκω ‘find’; ἔθ’ is ‘still, any longer’, and μῆτις is ‘plan, craft’.

sentences.t:
μάλα δ’ ὀτρύνουσι τοκῆες
γήμασθ’, ἀσχαλάᾳ δὲ πάϊς βίοτον κατεδόντων,
γιγνώσκων·
sentences.i: and my parents urge me strongly to marry, and my son, understanding it, is vexed at those who eat up his livelihood;
sentences.n: ὀτρύνουσι is ‘urge’, with γήμασθαι (aorist infinitive middle, ‘to marry’, said of a woman) as its object; τοκῆες is ‘parents’, the same word as in line 105. ἀσχαλάᾳ is ‘is vexed’ (ἀσχαλάω), with the genitive participle κατεδόντων ‘of those who eat up’ (present participle of κατέδω), whose object is βίοτον ‘livelihood’. πάϊς is Epic παῖς, ‘child’, her son. γιγνώσκων is ‘understanding’.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γὰρ ἀνὴρ οἷός τε μάλιστα
οἴκου κήδεσθαι, τῷ τε Ζεὺς κῦδος ὀπάζει.
sentences.l:
for already he is a man such as best
to care for the house, one to whom Zeus grants glory.
sentences.i: for he is by now a man best able to look after the household, a man to whom Zeus grants glory.
sentences.n: ἤδη γάρ ‘for by now’ gives the reason for his understanding. οἷός τε with an infinitive is ‘such as to, able to’, here with κήδεσθαι ‘take care of’ and the genitive οἴκου ‘the house’, strengthened by μάλιστα ‘best’. τῷ is the article used as a relative, ‘to whom’, with τε of the general statement; ὀπάζει is ‘grants, bestows’, with κῦδος ‘glory’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὥς μοι εἰπὲ τεὸν γένος, ὁππόθεν ἐσσί.
sentences.l: But even so tell me your birth, from where you are.
sentences.i: But even so, tell me of your birth, and where you come from.
sentences.n: Having explained her plight, she asks again. ἀλλὰ καὶ ὥς is ‘but even so’ (ὥς the adverb, ‘thus’); μοι is ‘to me’, and εἰπέ the imperative of εἶπον ‘tell’. τεόν is the Epic form of σόν ‘your’, γένος is ‘birth, family’, and ἐσσί the Epic form of εἶ ‘you are’; ὁππόθεν is ‘from where’, in an indirect question.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ ἀπὸ δρυός ἐσσι παλαιφάτου οὐδ’ ἀπὸ πέτρης.
sentences.l: for not from an oak of ancient report are you, nor from a rock.”
sentences.i: for you do not come from some oak of the old stories, or from a rock.”
sentences.n: A proverbial reason: no one is born of an oak or a rock, so everyone has a family to name. ἀπὸ δρυός … ἀπὸ πέτρης is ‘from an oak … from a rock’, an old tale said of men; παλαίφατος is ‘spoken of long ago, of ancient report’. οὐ … οὐδ’ is ‘not … nor’. Penelope’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: The formula of line 106 again: τὴν … ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη, ‘answering her, addressed’, with the stock epithet πολύμητις ‘of many wiles’. Odysseus now answers her demand for his family, and this part carries his account as far as line 202.

sentences.t:
ὦ γύναι αἰδοίη Λαερτιάδεω Ὀδυσῆος,
οὐκέτ’ ἀπολλήξεις τὸν ἐμὸν γόνον ἐξερέουσα;
sentences.l:
“O wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes, revered one,
no longer will you leave off, asking out my stock?
sentences.i: “Revered wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes, will you never stop asking about my family?
sentences.n: ὦ γύναι αἰδοίη Λαερτιάδεω Ὀδυσῆος is ‘O revered wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes’: the genitives Λαερτιάδεω (‘son of Laertes’) and Ὀδυσῆος depend on γύναι, and αἰδοίη ‘revered’ agrees with it. οὐκέτ’ ἀπολλήξεις; is ‘will you no longer leave off?’, said with impatience, ‘will you never stop?’; ἀπολλήγω takes the participle ἐξερέουσα ‘asking out’ (the same family as ἐξερέεινε, 116), and γόνος is ‘offspring, stock’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔκ τοι ἐρέω·
sentences.l: But I will speak out plainly to you;
sentences.i: But I will tell you plainly;
sentences.n: A tmesis: ἐκ … ἐρέω is the single verb ἐξερέω, ‘I will speak out’, with the preverb ἐκ set before τοι (σοι ‘to you’). Odysseus gives way, but warns her at once that the telling will hurt.

sentences.t:
ἦ μέν μ’ ἀχέεσσί γε δώσεις
πλείοσιν ἢ ἔχομαι·
sentences.l:
truly you will give me to griefs
more than I am held by;
sentences.i: you will surely give me over to more griefs than already hold me;
sentences.n: ἦ μέν is ‘truly’, γε adds stress. δώσεις μ’ ἀχέεσσι is ‘you will give me over to griefs’ (ἀχέεσσι, dative plural of ἄχος ‘grief’); πλείοσιν is ‘more’, and ἢ ἔχομαι is ‘than I am held (by)’, the passive of ἔχω, with ‘griefs’ understood.

sentences.t:
ἡ γὰρ δίκη, ὁππότε πάτρης
ἧς ἀπέῃσιν ἀνὴρ τόσσον χρόνον ὅσσον ἐγὼ νῦν,
πολλὰ βροτῶν ἐπὶ ἄστε’ ἀλώμενος, ἄλγεα πάσχων·
sentences.i: for that is how it is whenever a man has been away from his own fatherland as long as I have been now, wandering over many cities of mortals and suffering pains;
sentences.n: ἡ γὰρ δίκη is ‘for that is the way of it’ (δίκη, ‘right, custom’, here ‘the way things go’). ὁππότε … ἀπέῃσιν is a general ‘whenever … he is away’ (subjunctive of ἄπειμι); ἧς is the possessive ‘his own’, agreeing with πάτρης ‘fatherland’, not the relative. τόσσον … ὅσσον is ‘as long … as’, with χρόνον. ἄστε’ is the elided Epic plural of ἄστυ ‘town, city’, and ἀλώμενος ‘wandering’ and ἄλγεα πάσχων ‘suffering pains’ describe the man.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὣς ἐρέω ὅ μ’ ἀνείρεαι ἠδὲ μεταλλᾷς.
sentences.l: But even so I will tell what you ask me and inquire after.
sentences.i: But even so I will tell you what you ask me and inquire after.
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὥς is ‘but even so’ again, as in line 162. ὅ μ’ is ὅ με, ‘what … me’, the object of both verbs. ἀνείρεαι is ‘you ask’ (ἀνείρομαι, the same verb as ἀνέρομαι), and μεταλλᾷς is ‘you inquire after’ (μεταλλάω, contracted from μεταλλάεις; Odysseus used the same verb in line 115).

sentences.t:
Κρήτη τις γαῖ’ ἔστι, μέσῳ ἐνὶ οἴνοπι πόντῳ,
καλὴ καὶ πίειρα, περίρρυτος·
sentences.l:
There is a certain land, Crete, in the middle of the wine-faced open-sea,
fine and rich, flowed-around;
sentences.i: There is a land called Crete, in the middle of the sea that has the look of wine, beautiful and rich, with the sea running all round it;
sentences.n: His tale of Crete begins. Κρήτη τις γαῖ’ ἔστι is ‘there is a certain land, Crete’. μέσῳ ἐνὶ οἴνοπι πόντῳ is ‘in the middle of the wine-faced open sea’: οἴνοψ, ‘wine-faced’, is the stock epithet of the sea and πόντος the open sea. πίειρα is ‘rich’ (feminine of πίων), and περίρρυτος ‘flowed round’ (περί and ῥέω), said of an island with the sea running all round it.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἄνθρωποι
πολλοί, ἀπειρέσιοι, καὶ ἐννήκοντα πόληες.
sentences.l:
and in it men
many, past counting, and ninety cities.
sentences.i: It has many men, countless numbers, and ninety cities.
sentences.n: ἐν here is an adverb, ‘in it’, with no verb expressed (‘in it are men …’). ἀπειρέσιοι is ‘past counting, countless’, from the same root as ἀπείρων ‘boundless’ in line 107; ἐννήκοντα is the Epic ‘ninety’ (Attic ἐνενήκοντα), and πόληες the Epic nominative plural of πόλις ‘city’.

sentences.t: ἄλλη δ’ ἄλλων γλῶσσα μεμιγμένη·
sentences.l: and different the tongue of different peoples, mingled together;
sentences.i: and their tongues are mingled together, a different speech for each people;
sentences.n: ἄλλη δ’ ἄλλων γλῶσσα is ‘one tongue (belongs) to some, another to others’: the pairing says that each people has its own speech, and μεμιγμένη, perfect passive participle of μίγνυμι ‘mix’, says that the whole is a mixture. The peoples are listed in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἐν μὲν Ἀχαιοί,
ἐν δ’ Ἐτεόκρητες μεγαλήτορες, ἐν δὲ Κύδωνες,
Δωριέες τε τριχάϊκες δῖοί τε Πελασγοί.
sentences.l:
in it Achaeans,
and in it great-spirited Eteocretans, and in it Cydonians,
and Dorians of three tribes and heavenly Pelasgians.
sentences.i: there are Achaeans, and great-spirited Eteocretans, and Cydonians, and Dorians in their three tribes, and heavenly Pelasgians.
sentences.n: A list of peoples, each with ἐν ‘in it’. Ἐτεόκρητες is ‘true Cretans’ (ἐτεός ‘true’), μεγαλήτορες ‘great-spirited’; Κύδωνες are the Cydonians and Δωριέες the Dorians. τριχάϊκες is a word whose meaning is not known: ‘in three tribes’ and ‘with waving plumes’ are both ancient guesses, and ‘of three tribes’ takes only the first. δῖοι is the stock ‘heavenly’, here of the Pelasgians.

sentences.t:
τῇσι δ’ ἐνὶ Κνωσός, μεγάλη πόλις, ἔνθα τε Μίνως
ἐννέωρος βασίλευε Διὸς μεγάλου ὀαριστής,
πατρὸς ἐμοῖο πατήρ, μεγαθύμου Δευκαλίωνος
Δευκαλίων δ’ ἐμὲ τίκτε καὶ Ἰδομενῆα ἄνακτα·
sentences.i: Among them is Cnossus, a great city, where Minos reigned in nine-year terms, the confidant of great Zeus and father of my father, great-hearted Deucalion. Deucalion begot me and lord Idomeneus;
sentences.n: Odysseus gives his Cretan descent. τῇσι ‘among them’ means the ninety cities, and Κνωσός is Cnossus. ἐννέωρος, ‘nine-yeared’, is of uncertain sense (‘for nine-year periods’ and ‘at nine years old’ have both been proposed); ὀαριστής is ‘confidant’, from ὀαρίζω ‘talk intimately’. In πατρὸς ἐμοῖο πατήρ, μεγαθύμου Δευκαλίωνος the genitive ‘of great-hearted Deucalion’ stands in apposition to πατρὸς ἐμοῖο: Minos is father of the speaker’s father, Deucalion. τίκτε is the unaugmented ‘begot’. The edition prints no stop at the end of line 180.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν ἐν νήεσσι κορωνίσιν Ἴλιον εἴσω
ᾤχεθ’ ἅμ’ Ἀτρείδῃσιν, ἐμοὶ δ’ ὄνομα κλυτὸν Αἴθων,
ὁπλότερος γενεῇ·
sentences.i: But he went off to Ilium in curved ships with the sons of Atreus, and my famous name is Aethon, the younger by birth;
sentences.n: ὁ μέν is Idomeneus, set against ἐμοὶ δέ ‘but to me’. νήεσσι κορωνίσιν is ‘in curved ships’ (κορωνίς, ‘curved’), Ἴλιον εἴσω ‘to within Ilium’, ᾤχεθ’ (ᾤχετο, from οἴχομαι) ‘went off’, and Ἀτρείδῃσιν ‘with the sons of Atreus’. The name Αἴθων is the same word as the adjective αἴθων ‘blazing, tawny’. ὁπλότερος γενεῇ is ‘younger by birth’, a dative of respect, said of the speaker.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ ἄρα πρότερος καὶ ἀρείων.
sentences.l: and he, indeed, was the elder and the better.
sentences.i: while he was the elder, and the better man.
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ is Idomeneus again. πρότερος, ‘earlier’, here means the elder, born before; ἀρείων is the comparative of ἀγαθός, ‘better’, which in a warrior has the sense ‘braver’.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ Ὀδυσῆα ἐγὼν ἰδόμην καὶ ξείνια δῶκα.
sentences.l: There I saw Odysseus, and gave the things due to guests.
sentences.i: There I saw Odysseus and gave him the hospitality due to guests.
sentences.n: Odysseus now speaks of ‘Odysseus’ in the third person, as a man he once entertained in Crete, while his wife listens. ἰδόμην is the Epic aorist middle of ὁράω ‘I saw’, ξείνια are ‘the things due to guests’ and δῶκα ‘I gave’ (aorist of δίδωμι). ἔνθ’ is ‘there’, in Crete.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ τὸν Κρήτηνδε κατήγαγεν ἲς ἀνέμοιο,
ἱέμενον Τροίηνδε παραπλάγξασα Μαλειῶν·
sentences.l:
for indeed him to Crete brought down the force of the wind,
as he was setting out for Troy, driving him aside from Malea;
sentences.i: For the force of the wind had brought him down to Crete when he was bound for Troy, driving him off course from Malea;
sentences.n: ἲς ἀνέμοιο is ‘the force of the wind’, a periphrasis for the wind itself (ἀνέμοιο is the old genitive of ἄνεμος), the subject of κατήγαγεν ‘brought down’. Κρήτηνδε and Τροίηνδε are ‘to Crete’ and ‘to Troy’ (-δε of direction); ἱέμενον is ‘making for’. παραπλάγξασα is feminine because ἲς is, ‘having driven aside’, with the genitive Μαλειῶν ‘from Malea’, the cape at the south of the Peloponnese.

sentences.t:
στῆσε δ’ ἐν Ἀμνισῷ, ὅθι τε σπέος Εἰλειθυίης,
ἐν λιμέσιν χαλεποῖσι, μόγις δ’ ὑπάλυξεν ἀέλλας.
sentences.l:
and it stopped him at Amnisus, where is the cave of Eileithyia,
in hard harbours, and scarcely he escaped the blasts.
sentences.i: and held him at Amnisus, where the cave of Eileithyia is, in hard harbours, and he barely escaped the storms.
sentences.n: στῆσε has the force of the wind as its subject and Odysseus (his ships) as an unspoken object: it made him stop. Ἀμνισός is a place on the coast of Crete, and Εἰλείθυια the goddess of childbirth. χαλεποῖσι is ‘hard (to enter)’; ὑπάλυξεν, aorist of ὑπαλύσκω, is ‘escaped from under’, with ἀέλλας ‘blasts, storms’; μόγις is ‘scarcely, with difficulty’.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δ’ Ἰδομενῆα μετάλλα ἄστυδ’ ἀνελθών·
sentences.l: At once for Idomeneus he asked, to the town having gone up;
sentences.i: He went up to the town at once and asked after Idomeneus;
sentences.n: The subject, ‘he’, is Odysseus, as in the lines before. μετάλλα is the unaugmented imperfect of μεταλλάω ‘inquire after’ (the same verb as in lines 115 and 171); ἄστυδ’ is ‘to the town’ (-δε of direction, elided), with ἀνελθών ‘having gone up’.

sentences.t: ξεῖνον γάρ οἱ ἔφασκε φίλον τ’ ἔμεν αἰδοῖόν τε.
sentences.l: for a guest-friend to him he kept saying he was, both dear and revered.
sentences.i: for he kept saying that Idomeneus was his guest-friend, dear and revered.
sentences.n: The reason he asked for Idomeneus. ἔφασκε is the iterative of φημί, ‘kept saying’; ἔμεν is the Epic infinitive of εἰμί ‘to be’, and its unspoken subject is Idomeneus, so ξεῖνον φίλον τ’ … αἰδοῖόν τε is ‘a guest-friend, both dear and revered’. οἱ, ‘to him’, is Odysseus. ξεῖνος here is the guest-friend of the old reciprocal bond.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἤδη δεκάτη ἢ ἑνδεκάτη πέλεν ἠὼς
οἰχομένῳ σὺν νηυσὶ κορωνίσιν Ἴλιον εἴσω.
sentences.l:
And for him already a tenth or an eleventh dawn was,
he having gone with curved ships to Ilium within.
sentences.i: It was already the tenth or the eleventh dawn since he had gone off with his curved ships to Ilium.
sentences.n: τῷ is Idomeneus: ‘for him it was already the tenth or the eleventh dawn’, a count of days since he left. πέλεν is the unaugmented imperfect of πέλω ‘was’. οἰχομένῳ (from οἴχομαι, ‘gone’) agrees with τῷ, ‘he having gone’, with σὺν νηυσὶ κορωνίσιν ‘with curved ships’ and Ἴλιον εἴσω ‘to Ilium’, as in line 182.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ πρὸς δώματ’ ἄγων ἐῢ ἐξείνισσα,
ἐνδυκέως φιλέων, πολλῶν κατὰ οἶκον ἐόντων·
sentences.l:
Him I, to my house leading, well entertained,
kindly welcoming, many things being in the house;
sentences.i: I took him to my house and entertained him well, welcoming him kindly, since there was plenty in the house;
sentences.n: ἄγων … ἐξείνισσα is ‘leading … I entertained’ (ξενίζω ‘entertain as a guest’, the Epic aorist with doubled σ), and ἐῢ is the Epic form of εὖ ‘well’. ἐνδυκέως is ‘kindly’, φιλέων ‘welcoming’ (the host’s φιλέω). πολλῶν … ἐόντων is a genitive absolute, ‘many things being in the house’, saying that he could afford it.

sentences.t:
καί οἱ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἑτάροις, οἳ ἅμ’ αὐτῷ ἕποντο,
δημόθεν ἄλφιτα δῶκα καὶ αἴθοπα οἶνον ἀγείρας
καὶ βοῦς ἱρεύσασθαι, ἵνα πλησαίατο θυμόν.
sentences.i: And to his other companions too, who had followed with him, I gave barley-meal and the wine that has the look of fire, which I gathered from the land, and oxen to slaughter, so that they might satisfy their hearts.
sentences.n: καί οἱ … ἑτάροις is ‘also to his other companions’ (οἱ is a possessive dative, ‘his’); οἳ ἅμ’ αὐτῷ ἕποντο is ‘who followed along with him’ (ἕποντο, unaugmented imperfect of ἕπομαι). δημόθεν is ‘from the δῆμος’, that is from the community’s contributions, kept here as ‘from the land’; ἀγείρας is ‘having collected’. αἴθοπα οἶνον is the stock ‘fire-faced wine’. ἱρεύσασθαι is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to slaughter (for themselves)’, and ἵνα πλησαίατο is the optative of purpose, ‘that they might fill’.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δυώδεκα μὲν μένον ἤματα δῖοι Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.l: There twelve days stayed the heavenly Achaeans;
sentences.i: There the heavenly Achaeans stayed for twelve days;
sentences.n: δυώδεκα is ‘twelve’, ἤματα ‘days’ (accusative of duration), and μένον the unaugmented imperfect ‘stayed’. δῖοι Ἀχαιοί is a stock phrase, ‘heavenly Achaeans’, translated every time like δῖος of Odysseus; here the Achaeans are Odysseus and his companions.

sentences.t:
εἴλει γὰρ Βορέης ἄνεμος μέγας οὐδ’ ἐπὶ γαίῃ
εἴα ἵστασθαι, χαλεπὸς δέ τις ὤρορε δαίμων.
sentences.l:
for the North Wind, a great wind, was shutting them in, and not upon the land
allowed them to stand, and some harsh power had stirred it up.
sentences.i: for the great North Wind kept them shut in and would not let them stand upon the land, since some harsh power had roused it.
sentences.n: Why they stayed. εἴλει is the imperfect of εἴλω ‘shut in, hem in’; εἴα is the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’, with the infinitive ἵστασθαι ‘to stand’ and οὐδ’ ‘and not’. Βορέης ἄνεμος is ‘the North Wind’, with μέγας ‘great’. χαλεπός is ‘harsh’, δαίμων ‘some power’, and ὤρορε is the Epic reduplicated aorist of ὄρνυμι, ‘roused, stirred up’.

sentences.t: τῇ τρισκαιδεκάτῃ δ’ ἄνεμος πέσε, τοὶ δ’ ἀνάγοντο.
sentences.l: On the thirteenth the wind fell, and they put out to sea.
sentences.i: On the thirteenth day the wind dropped, and they put out to sea.
sentences.n: τῇ τρισκαιδεκάτῃ is ‘on the thirteenth’ (a dative of time, with ‘day’ understood); πέσε is the unaugmented aorist of πίπτω, ‘fell, dropped’, said of the wind; τοί is the article used as a pronoun, ‘they’, and ἀνάγοντο, imperfect middle, is ‘were putting out to sea’. Odysseus’ speech does not end here; it runs on into the next part, so there is no closing quotation mark.
